situation:
You and your partner are the director of marketing and the director of client services at CARRYWELL LOGISTICS PARTNERS, a third-party logistics provider that warehouses and ships freight for regional retailers. The president (judge), the third generation of the family to run the company, has asked the two of you to recommend how Carrywell should handle a problem that reaches both its largest account and the promise its sales story rests on.

Carrywell has moved freight for almost forty years, and what it sells is a service rather than a product on a shelf. Its competitive advantage in every proposal is the same line: a fully certified workforce, trained each year in cargo security, hazardous materials handling, and dock safety. That claim is why shippers choose Carrywell over larger national carriers quoting lower rates, and the company's client relationships are built on it.

The training itself is not getting done. The annual program moved online three years ago, and roughly a third of the warehouse workforce finishes it. Crews start modules between loads and abandon them; supervisors chase completions and then stop chasing. The few crew leads who do finish every year have never been acknowledged for it. Nothing has gone wrong on a dock yet, and nothing about that is guaranteed.

RIDGEPORT OUTFITTERS, Carrywell's largest client, renews next month, and its contract requires certified completion figures with the renewal paperwork. Operations has proposed a condensed sign-off session run on paid shift time before the deadline. It would put completion at full marks this quarter, protect the renewal, and let the marketing claim stand, but it would spend the year's entire training budget on an hour that teaches very little.

The deeper recertification due next quarter would then have no money and no appetite behind it, and the crews would have learned that the training is paperwork. The alternative is to give Ridgeport the real figures now and run the full program properly across two quarters. That protects the claim Carrywell makes and the risk sitting on the dock, but it puts the renewal, and the account, in question.

The president (judge) wants your recommendation on which course Carrywell should take, what each one costs, whether the certified-workforce claim can keep appearing in the company's marketing, and how the crews should be brought into the decision. The president (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you both when your presentation and questions are finished.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president of CARRYWELL LOGISTICS PARTNERS. Business background is the same as the situation above. You called this meeting because the annual compliance training almost nobody finishes is now tied to the renewal of the company's largest account and to the certified-workforce claim the company markets. You want the participant team's recommendation on whether to run the condensed sign-off session before the renewal deadline or give the client the real figures and rebuild the program across two quarters.

You will greet the participant team and ask them to share their ideas. Ask the following questions after their presentation:
judgeQuestions: If we do what you are recommending, who ends up carrying the cost of it — the crews, the client, or us?
Can we defend putting the cost there if someone asks us about it?
